name: Amrize Ltd

profile.description: Amrize is the largest cement producer in North America and a major supplier of aggregates, ready-mix concrete, and building-envelope products (commercial and residential roofing, insulation), spun off from Holcim in June 2025. It operates two segments: Building Materials (Q3 2026 revenue $2.84B, 33.0% segment EBITDA margin) and Building Envelope (Q3 2026 revenue $929M) [1]. Chairman and CEO Jan Jenisch, former Holcim and Sika CEO, leads the company; Q3 2026 revenue rose 2.2% to $3.77B and FY2026 revenue guidance is $12.2-12.4B [1][2].

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): Amrize's main change in five years is structural — the 2025 spin-off from Holcim and bolt-on acquisitions such as PB Materials and Rapid Redi-Mix (Dallas-Fort Worth), which added $77M to Q3 2026 revenue [1]. The product set (cement, aggregates, ready-mix, roofing) looks much as it did five years ago. AI Deployment (0/2): The Q3 2026 release and investor materials contain no AI products or quantified AI savings; the closest item is the ASPIRE cost program ($73M saved year to date against an $80M 2026 target), which is not attributed to AI [1]. Market Share (2/2): Amrize is the largest cement producer in North America, and Q3 2026 aggregates pricing rose 6.9% with Building Materials margin expanding 30bps to 33.0%, showing pricing power that comes with leadership [1][2]. Pipeline (1/2): Management points to data-center and energy-project 'mega-trends' and strong commercial roofing system sales into data-center and industrial projects, but names no specific new products or capacity with dated revenue [1]. R&D Intensity (0/1): No meaningful R&D disclosure; the company is a heavy-materials producer with spending focused on ~$900M capex rather than research [1].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): Amrize presents itself as 'building North America' and says it brings innovation to what it does — clear on what it does and where, but not a distinct purpose beyond being a scale building-materials supplier [3]. Community Impact (0/2): Searches found no specific Amrize foundation, community programs, or dollar figures for community investment since the spin-off [4]. Employee Retention (0/2): No retention, turnover, or tenure data was found for the 19,000-employee company, and no Glassdoor data surfaced [3]. Insider Buying (0/2): No evidence of meaningful net insider buying in the last 12 months was found; capital returns went through the company's $1B buyback, completed October 28, 2026 [1].

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Calculated mechanically as a Growth stock (dividend yield of 1.06% is below the 2% Dividend threshold) [5]. D/E of 54.8% (1.00), Forward P/E of 15.7 (1.00), and PEG of 1.09 (0.955, 2x weight) score near the maximum; ROE of 9.7% (0.648, 2x) and profit margin of 10.2% (0.511) are below target [5]. Revenue growth is the main weakness: YoY revenue growth is 2.2% (0.740), and the 3-year revenue CAGR derived from reported revenue ($10.73B in 2022 to $11.82B in 2025, 3.3%) scores 0.553 at 2x weight. A 5-year figure was not available because the company was spun off in 2025 [5]. Weighted sum 7.56/10 rounds to 8. Net leverage is 1.8x ($5.55B net debt), and daily dollar volume of about $172M (4.16M shares x $41.38) easily clears the liquidity floor [1][5].

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (8/9): Amrize quarries limestone and aggregates, fires cement kilns, and delivers ready-mix and roofing to job sites. These are heavy, local, physical operations that AI cannot substitute, and freight economics protect regional market positions [1]. AI is a demand tailwind rather than a threat: management credits data-center and energy projects for long-term construction demand, and commercial roofing volumes were strong on data-center and industrial work in Q3 2026 [1]. AI Opportunity (0/1): Amrize does not disclose any revenue specifically attributed to AI (for example, a data-center revenue figure), so the tiebreaker point is not awarded.

infinite_game.summary: Amrize is a well-run, scale-focused materials company whose story so far is about financial results: margin programs (ASPIRE), a $1B buyback completed within about 16 months of listing, and acquisitions that add to EPS [1]. Sinek would credit Jan Jenisch's record of reshaping Holcim and his stated trust-based leadership. But a one-year-old spin-off has not yet shown a Just Cause tested by a downturn, and its language is about pricing, volumes, and returns rather than a future worth sacrificing for [1][3].

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): 'Building North America' describes a market, not a future state people would sacrifice for. Q3 2026 messaging centers on 'resilient results', price increases, and EPS accretion [1][3]. Sustainability-oriented products that Holcim emphasized under Jenisch are not mentioned in the Q3 2026 release, so the purpose does not visibly shape Amrize's public story yet [1].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): Jenisch has described building a culture of trust in which employee feedback is valued and responsibility is delegated to the most capable people [3]. Amrize's leadership team is drawn from long-time Holcim executives, which gives continuity [3]. However, no retention or employee-sentiment data exists yet for Amrize, and an aggressive cost program ($80M 2026 ASPIRE target) puts pressure on the organization [1].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Amrize's communications stress being 'the largest' building-materials player in North America and gaining share through acquisitions [1][3]. No management commentary was found that treats rivals such as Vulcan, Martin Marietta, or CRH as benchmarks for self-improvement.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Separating the North American business from Holcim to create a US-listed company was a major structural decision, and Jenisch previously reshaped Holcim's portfolio toward building solutions such as roofing [2][3]. Amrize itself still operates the same cement-and-aggregates core, so the change is adaptation within its industry rather than reinvention [1].

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Leadership kept investing about $900M in 2026 capex and continued acquisitions through a weather-hit year in which cement volumes fell 4.2% in Q3 [1]. Completing a $1B buyback during 2026 (retiring about 4% of shares) while free cash flow was negative year to date (-$551M) is a capital-return choice that a finite player would make, which offsets the credit [1].

investment_thesis: Amrize is North America's largest cement producer and trades at 15.7x forward earnings with a PEG of 1.09, low leverage (D/E 54.8%, 1.8x net leverage), and strong pricing: Q3 2026 aggregates prices rose 6.9% and the Building Materials margin expanded to 33.0% even as weather cut cement volumes 4.2% [1][5]. Net income grew 3.3% to $558M in Q3, nine-month revenue grew 5.0% to $9.45B, and the company returned about $1.1B to shareholders through Q3, including a $1B buyback completed October 28 [1]. Data-center, energy, and infrastructure construction give multi-year demand support for a business with no AI substitution risk [1].
thesis_continued: The bear case is slow organic growth and cash conversion. Q3 revenue grew only 2.2% (helped by $77M of acquisitions), adjusted EPS was flat at $1.05, and FY2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $2.95-3.05B implies little growth [1]. Building Envelope margin fell 410bps to 19.6% on freight and raw-material inflation, and management pushed price-cost recovery into 2027. Residential shingle demand is weak due to fewer storms and slow existing-home sales [1]. Free cash flow was negative $551M through nine months while the company spent $750M on buybacks and $467M on acquisitions, so continued returns depend on Q4 cash generation and debt capacity [1]. ROE of 9.7% and a 3.3% three-year revenue CAGR show a mature, cyclical business [5].
key_catalysts: Q4 2026 seasonal cash generation reversing the $551M year-to-date free-cash-flow use, which would support the up-to-$0.44 annual dividend and further buybacks after the completed $1B program [1]
Data-center and energy-project construction lifting cement and commercial roofing volumes, which management names as long-term demand 'mega-trends' [1]
Building Envelope price-cost recovery in 2027 restoring segment margin from 19.6% toward prior-year levels near 23.7% [1]
key_risks: Continued cement volume weakness (down 4.2% in Q3 2026) if weather or a construction slowdown persists, with fixed-cost kilns magnifying the margin impact [1]
Building Envelope margin compression from freight and raw-material inflation, with residential shingle demand tied to storm activity and existing-home sales [1]
Debt-funded capital returns and acquisitions (net debt $5.55B) while year-to-date free cash flow is negative, reducing flexibility in a cyclical downturn [1]
